speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I promised to make a statement in connection with the anti-cancer hormone treatment developed by Doctors V. A. and V. V. Mirko-vich.
The Department of National Health and Welfare has received an interim report from the Ontario Cancer Treatment and Research Foundation on their investigation of the clinical use in Mexico of a product designated as an anti-cancer hormone developed by these two doctors. During the last week in May two senior consultants of the Ontario Cancer Treatment and Research Foundation visited Dr. A. G. Andrade, of Vera Cruz, Mexico, who was reported to have administered this material to a number of patients. The physicians from the foundation examined available records and diagnostic materials. They have extracted and reported on the available data, but since this was inadequate to establish the purported claims for the anti-cancer hormone they have requested additional data from Dr. Andrade. This will include photographs, pathological slides and x-ray plates for evaluation to confirm the reported diagnosis and reported clinical responses.
During 1963 and 1964 Dr. Andrade treated a total of five patients with a product designated as anti-cancer hormone supplied personally by the Doctors Mirkovich. Of the five patients two have died, two were examined by the Canadian consultants, and the fifth person was reported to be alive but was not seen by the Canadian physicians. Of the two patients who died, one child was reported to have been suffering from lymphocythic leukemia and the other patient was reported to have been suffering from osteogenic sarcoma.
Of the two patients examined by the Canadian consultants, one child who was reported to have a neuro-fibrosarcoma of the mouth had been treated with radiation and a chemotherapeutic agent in addition to the anti-cancer hormone. The reported response could have been due to the radiotherapy and the known chemotherapeutic agent. Additional data have been requested in this case.
The second patient seen was a woman who was reported to have a malignant lesion of the tibia. Specimens from this patient had also been examined by two pathologists in Mexico, one from the National Cancer Institute of Mexico, both of whom diagnosed the

The data supplied in the interim report have been reviewed by the medical staff of the food and drug directorate. In their opinion the scientific information available to date has failed to demonstrate any curative or palliative action of A.C.H. in the treatment of cancer. I should add that Dr. Matthew Dymond proposes to include the following paragraph in the statement he is making in Toronto today:
My advisers agree that the evidence so far obtained is insufficient at the present time to justify the claims of the Drs. Mirkovich that A.C.H. is of value in cancer treatment. They submitted the interim report and are collecting the additional information in order to complete this document.

Sir, I think the solution to this problem lies in making available larger amounts in unconditional grants to the various universities than have hitherto been passed on to them so that they in turn may reduce the amount of the annual fees.
Today fees have risen to such a point that they are almost prohibitive. In my day $35 or $40 a year represented the amount of fees required. All that is changed and many students today find it difficult to carry on at the rates which now exist and which are increasing year by year. I believe that as the parliament of Canada makes available increased grants to universities, as it must-there is no escaping that-there is no reason why those sums should not be in the form of conditional grants with a provision that the amount of the fees paid by university students should be reduced. There is no interference there with the authority of the provinces over education. Nobody has to accept a grant. But if a grant is accepted it should be passed on in part for the benefit of the students.
These are just a few suggestions I wanted to make in a desire to bring about further changes and in conformity with the lead given by the Minister without Portfolio. In other words, they are intended to improve this legislation by bringing about changes during the months that lie ahead.
We will never realize our national destiny unless we make education available to those who are able to profit from it. In the province of Ontario tremendous advances 23033-4312

Canada Student Loans Act have been made under the Robarts government. I think of what the minister of education, Hon. Mr. Davis, has done in setting up community colleges. This was an excellent step and one which I think should be followed across the nation for the benefit of all. I believe that only 7 per cent of those of university age are able to attend universities. Some 30 per cent have the necessary capacity. The failure to make available a university education for that 23 per cent is a national waste. No one today has to prove that an education is of benefit economically to the individual as well as to the nation. I do not intend to go into that aspect of the matter on this occasion but there are many statistics on it.
It will be said that anything done in this connection will cost money. Well, this is the kind of expenditure which will bring dividends to the nation as a whole. It is because of this that I place before the minister these few suggestions, assuring him that any steps taken which have full regard to the constitutional division of powers and will expand and develop educational benefits will receive support.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make three short observations at this point. Needless to say, the first is that I am happy to lend my support to this very popular piece of legislation. The proof of its popularity lies in the use that has been made of it. I know it is administered by the provinces but I am sure the federal government has a great deal to say about its administration.
Second, at present a new approach is being taken to increase the facilities of universities by adopting the summer semester idea whereby a student can do a year and a half's work in one year by making full use of a university during the summer. This idea has been put into practice at the University of Guelph in my riding, but it makes it necessary for a student to have more money over a one year period since he has to attend three semesters rather than two as in the past. I would like to be assured that this is taken into account by the various provinces.
The third observation I wish to make concerns the application form which a student and his parents must fill out when applying for a loan. I have before me one such application form from the province of Ontario which seeks some very personal and confidential information, including a statement of resources to be completed by the parents. It asks for information concerning salaries and wages, total income, other income, life insurance, whether their home is owned by themselves, its present market value, the amount of unpaid mortgage, details of other real estate and details of their bank accounts, both personal and savings.

I realize that such information is necessary in order to determine whether a student is in need of funds and I would quite agree with such an application form being retained in the hands of the banker who administers the loan, but when the information becomes generally known to university officials, including the registrar and everybody in his office, this is a mistake. Such confidential information should be retained in the hands of a banker who is in the habit of treating all such matters personally and confidentially. Again, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say that I lend my support to this very fine piece of legislation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, many hon. members have taken advantage of the debate on the Canada student loans bill to express their views on education and educational policy generally. I have listened with very great interest to this debate. I think it has been a very useful one and has shown a remarkable unanimity of view among the parties in this house in respect of the importance of education and the large part government aid to education is necessarily going to play in the future. As one of those who had difficulty in obtaining a university education and, like the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), had to resort to various means of financing, I can heartily sympathize with the desire of all members who have participated in this debate to be sure not that university education becomes more easily attainable but that all those who have the ability to benefit from a university education obtain it.
As I said on a previous occasion, this problem is not going to be solved simply by making university education freely available either without charge or with such aid as would make it possible for students to obtain it. The problem is much deeper than that; it extends below the university level. One of the most difficult and serious problems we face is ensuring that those students who should be able to benefit from a university education do in fact graduate from high school. So the problem is one of far reaching difficulty and complexity.
I also agree with those who have spoken who have mentioned the magnitude of the financial requirements to ensure that our young people are adequately educated. As Minister of Finance I am very conscious of that; I am very conscious of it in relation to federal-provincial discussions. This is a question which must be discussed with the provinces. It is, if not entirely, certainly their primary responsibility. It is primarily the responsibility of the provinces, but that does not discharge the federal government from the responsibility to see that adequate educational opportunities are available to all Canadians. It does mean that we must work together with the provinces to achieve these desirable goals.
The Leader of the Opposition referred to the comments made by my colleague the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Turner). I am

June 23, 1966

Canada Student Loans Act not a parliamentarian of great experience like the Leader of the Opposition and therefore perhaps it did not shock me quite as much as it did the right hon. gentleman when my colleague got up and expressed some views about education and put forward some of his own personal suggestions as to how this legislation might be improved in the future. I do know that my colleague, as he said, supports this legislation, but like many of us in the cabinet he hopes that in the future it can be improved still further. He put forward some suggestions, which he has made privately in other places and which I was glad to hear him put forward in this house, about how in the future we might move to make this legislation even more useful than it has been to date.
In general, during this discussion there has been agreement in respect of the aims of the Canada student loans plan and the amendments which now are before the house for consideration. In order, I hope, to shorten discussion in committee I should like to provide some answers to questions which were asked during the debate on the resolution stage and on second reading. The Leader of the Opposition asked about the eligibility of students from other countries. The Canada Student Loans Act defines a qualifying student as, among other things, one who (a) is a Canadian citizen or (b) has been resident in Canada for a period of not less than one year and has declared that he intends to reside in Canada after he ceases to be a full-time student.
In practice this means that a non-Canadian may be eligible if he has landed immigrant status. It does not include students from other countries entering Canada on a student's visa. Students from other countries applying for a student's visa for study in Canada must sign a declaration that they have sufficient funds to support themselves while in Canada. This financial support, of course, may come from Canadian sources in the form of scholarships or assistance under such programs as the Colombo Plan, but it follows that such students are not in need of and do not qualify for student loans.
Hon. members may recall that when the Canada Student Loans Act was introduced in the house nearly two years ago the minister of finance stated at page 5443 of Hansard of July 14, 1964:
Students who are residents of other countries will not be eligible for loans under the Canada student loans plan. Students from the richer countries abroad who choose to study here will have
their own sources of finance; with our universities already crowded we do not consider we should offer them special inducements to come here. Students from the less developed countries may. of course, obtain educational assistance under several Canadian programs.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I might mention further on this point that in order to avoid hardship for immigrants who have been in Canada for not much more than a year the provinces have agreed upon a residence formula which includes the case of landed immigrants. I refer here to the report on residence, which is included in appendix A of Hansard for June 11, 1965. This report forms part of the federal-provincial agreed criteria which are being applied in the administration of the plan and to which I referred in my opening statement when the resolution was being debated.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) asked how the $58 million in the new basic loan provision is to be allocated among the provinces. The basic loan provision in the loan year 1965-66 will be allocated to all provinces and territories on the basis of population in the 18 to 24 year age group. The act provides that in subsequent years the basic allocation will be increased each year at the same rate as the estimated growth of the population in Canada in that same age group. This rate of increase has been about 5 per cent.
In addition to the basic loan provision, which is $58 million for this year, the bill provides for a discretionary amount equal to 20 per cent of the basic loan provision, that is, $11,600,000 in the current year, all or any part of which the Minister of Finance may allocate to any participating province where the demand for loans under the agreed criteria exceeds that province's basic allocation. As I explained in my statement on the resolution, this supplementary allocation provides the flexibility required to adjust allocations to the varying degrees of demand for student loans from province to province.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Basford) suggested that the regulations be amended to extend the interest and repayment free period for borrowers while serving with CUSO or The Company of Young Canadians. This question was also raised by other hon. members. Representations to this effect have been made on several occasions recently and have been given very careful consideration. Legal advice has been obtained to the effect that such a change could be made only through an amendment to the act, not by regulations.

June 23, 1966	COMMONS
The reason we did not bring forward a change in the act in order to provide for this kind of flexibility is this. The Canada student loans plan is a very general measure applying to all provinces but one, and the effectiveness of such a general measure depends to a large extent on the basic simplicity of the plan. It was never intended to cover all requirements of all students but to serve as a broad base in the student assistance field, to be supplemented by other governmental and private schemes which should cover more specific situations. Any provision to afford a particular group special treatment under the plan would inevitably lead to representations for similar treatment by other groups who, at least in their own views, consider themselves equally deserving of special treatment.
The act and the regulations in their present form provide a bank, of course, with a good deal of flexibility in setting repayment terms with due regard to a borrower's probable ability to repay his loan, and it would be quite within the spirit of the legislation if a bank scheduled the repayments of a candidate for The Company of Young Canadians or CUSO over the maximum period provided for in the legislation, namely, ten years from the month of graduation.
This could at least partially meet the problem raised in individual cases where the amount of the loan owed is relatively small. To the extent that there remains a problem it seem to me and to the government that it could be dealt with more appropriately and directly through the provision of funds to The Company of Young Canadians and to CUSO for the purpose of helping to meet financial problems of highly desirable volunteers who, because of certain financial obligations, would not be able to serve without such special assistance. That is the brief answer to the point. It does seem to us to be more suitable for the special needs of candidates for The Company of Young Canadians and CUSO to be met by those agencies rather than by any forgiveness or special treatment under the Canada student loans plan.
The hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) referred to opposition to the Canada Student Loans Act two years ago on the ground that education is under exclusive provincial jurisdiction. He asked whether the views of the new premier of Quebec had been ascertained and, if not, whether I intend to get in touch with the new premier in order to know whether his views are the same as his predecessor's.

The act provides that if the government of a province advises the minister before the beginning of a loan year, that is before July 1, that a provincial student loan plan will be in operation in that province in that loan year and that no appropriate authority for that province will be designated for the purposes of this act, the minister shall pay to that province an alternative amount calculated in accordance with section 12(2). I am bringing this provision of the act to the attention of the new Quebec premier.
Those were some of the main points that were raised. Toward the conclusion of the debate today and on several other occasions comments were made about changes that have been made by the government of Ontario in the administration of its bursary plan. I would not wish to give the impression that all the changes that have been made by the province of Ontario are exactly what we would have approved, but I do believe it is in the interests of the federal plan, and ultimately of the students themselves, to have student aid resources used in such a way that the limited amount of aid that is available, particularly bursary aid, will go as far as possible to meet students' needs. So where a province integrates the federal loan scheme with a provincial bursary scheme it is entirely within both the letter and the spirit of the federal plan to have the provinces decide how and in what ratio it wishes to meet the needs from loan and grant sources. We may wish to critize some provisions of the Ontario plan, but I did feel it desirable to say that in principle we do not find its plans to be unacceptable.
Comments were made by some hon. members about the extension of these loans to night students and summer course students. My colleague the Minister without Portfolio made this suggestion. I am sure that all of those who have had experience in attending night school will know that one of the main reasons for having student aid available in the form of loans or bursaries is to avoid night study by students, which is not a particularly satisfactory way of carrying on one's education. It seemed to me when I was a student, and I am sure this is so today, that the problem is not one of being able to finance the limited cost of night study. The purpose of the Canada Student Loans Act is to see that students can attend universities in the day time for full-time study.
We are prepared, of course, to have another look at this problem. As my colleague, the
June 23, 1966

Canada Student Loans Act Minister without Portfolio, knows, a great deal of part-time study is done in one of the great institutions in his city, Sir George Williams University, and that is a provincial rather than a federal matter. I do know that in the city of Toronto there is a good deal of night study going on and we have not by any means dropped our consideration of this question for the future.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
That hon. member also expressed concern over the lack of reciprocity between the Canada Student Loans Act and the Quebec student assistance plan. I am sure that hon. members will understand that this is a matter for negotiation between the province and the federal government. We have done some work and the agreement on residence that was worked out at a recent federal-provincial conference is evidence of the fact that we are concerned about the problem. Had it not been for the changes of government in various provinces in this country we would probably be engaged even now in discussing with the provinces this and other matters affecting educational policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this item replaces two items that have been in the tariff for a number of years and which provided free entry for a specified list of settlers' effects. The new item represents a consolidation and simplification of the former item. Previously the goods had to be owned abroad by the settler for at least six months in order to qualify for free entry. The first change of substance is that under the proposed item the goods must still be in his possession to be entitled to free entry but the six months' ownership requirement has been dropped. speechtext:
The hon. member for Edmonton West has raised a very pertinent question and one that has caused me a great deal of concern. Perhaps I might be permitted to give a general explanation and then talk about this particular activity.
When an activity is considered to be an act of manufacture or production for sales tax purposes, the person performing such activity must pay tax on the selling price of the products resulting from this activity. The general definition of manufacturer or producer in the Excise Tax Act is broad enough to encompass all activities resulting in the creation of new products, and also all rebuilding or remanufacturing of goods if the commodities involved are the property of the rebuilder or the remanufacturer and are sold in the same manner as new commodities. That is the present act before amendment.
Everyone who is engaged in production or manufacturing, whether he is remanufacturing something he owns or whether he is manufacturing a new article, is subject to sales tax. That is a well established principle of the Excise Tax Act and has been in effect for a long time. However, up until this amendment to the act the federal sales tax did not apply to services. This has sometimes caused problems in areas where services rendered to repair old commodities account for the major proportion of the value of the repaired articles. In such instances the persons repairing those commodities compete with vendors of the new commodities or of the rebuilt commodities that they already own.
In all fairness, and this is the underlying principle of this change, the tax should apply to the charges made for services. Certainly this is the case with tire retreading.
The hon. member will recall that in 1963 the act was amended to make it apply to the sale of stock tires owned by the retreader. It could not be applied, however, to the repair of old tires. The result was a rather untidy administrative position. Indeed, you can imagine the kind of tax avoidance that went on. Instead of buying a stock retread, a person would go to an establishment with an old casing and say: "If you build this up for me I will not have to pay tax." We decided this year to try to apply the tax fairly by applying it not only to the retreaded tires owned by the remanufacturer but also to the value added to tires brought in by a customer to have retreaded.

This is the basic philosophy underlying this change. I am free to admit to the hon. gentleman that it has caused a good deal of complaint. We have looked very carefully at these complaints because in a sense we have a choice of evils. Either we continue with the present inequitable and unsatisfactory situation or we change the law as we are now proposing, knowing full well that the administrative result is not going to be too satisfactory. We have come to a conclusion and that is why we are pressing this amendment on the ground that it is better to attempt to apply the law equitably by this amendment rather than continuing to suffer under the inequalities of the present law.

custom retreaded has an unfair advantage over one buying a stock tire.

speechtext: In order that there may be no misunderstanding, may I say it is my understanding that rebuilt engines are taxable as are rebuilt television sets and rebuilt refrigerators.

I shall accept the minister's correction in that regard. But I find it extraordinary that this principle of the extension of sales tax to a service is now countenanced. I submit that we shall have a sales tax on services generally next. Using the salami method, there will be a gradual extension slice by slice. I cannot for the life of me see why this is being done.
Let us consider the difference between a tire retreader and a manufacturer. What is the difference between the new tire manufacturer and the retreader? The new tire manufacturer uses 100 per cent new raw materials and builds a new tire of which he maintains ownership until the time of sale. The retreader uses material mainly supplied by the tire manufacturer and the proportion of the content of new material to the old material is about 15 per cent. If the retreader is retreading a custom tire he has no ownership whatsoever in the tire. In the case of the stock tire he does.
Let us consider the difference in the incidence, say, of tax on a new tire as opposed to a retread. The new tire manufacturer pays a tax of 11 per cent on approximately 60 per cent of the selling price of a new tire. Let us take as an example a popular, good quality tire which retails at about $30. The cost to the manufacturer is between $10 and $12. He puts it out to the wholesaler or distribution agency where it is sold to a dealer, garage or service station at between $16 and $18. The customer pays $30. But sales tax is paid at the manufacturer's level.
In the case of a stock retread there may be an allowance of $5 or $6 on a good quality used casing. The value of the retreading, labour and materials is between $9.75 and $10.50. The retreaded tire is then sold for

Excise Tax Act
about $16, and that is where the 11 per cent sales tax is levied. The sales tax on a retread is on a higher level than it is in the case of a new tire.
The minister talks about improper incidence of taxation. Of course it is. But it is on the retreaded tire, not on the new tire. The retreaded tire bears a far greater sales tax load.
Are there any ways of avoiding or reducing the tax? Yes, there are certain ways. Some tire manufacturers own retreading plants. A manufacturer will sell to his own company at a wholesale price, and this is where the sales tax is levied. The service store is not then obliged to collect sales tax from the consumer at the retail level. The new tire manufacturer with his own retreading subsidiary has a definite advantage over an independent, and there are some 600 Canadian-owned independents in this country today. There are approximately seven tire manufacturers in this country, all foreign-owned. The application of this tax therefore places an unfair burden on Canadian-owned industry.
I will admit that the tire manufacturers employ a large number of people. But so do the tire retreaders. If hon. members wish to know the incidence of this taxation in connection with truck tires, I have some figures before me.
We must remember also the difference between the big trucking operator who is entitled to discounts and the small operator who is not. The sales tax on retreaded tires falls much more heavily on the smaller operator than it does on the big operator who is in a position to get substantial fleet discounts. Thus again we see the unfair incidence of this tax.
I am sure the officials in charge of sales tax administration in the department are aware of many ways in which this tax becomes an administrative monstrosity. There is no way of checking the number of retreaded tires which may be diverted to used tire stocks unless the department has inspectors out every morning to check on tire production and sales.
Other methods could be raised. I must say frankly that this will likely lead to the ruination of an industry. Let us face it: The tire retreading industry exists because of the sheer economics of the difference between the price of a new and a retreaded tire. The minister knows the cost of a huge tire such as is used for a carrier or heavy-load earth

mover. Such tires cost thousands of dollars. They go back to the shops for custom rebuilding. Why impose this tax on the custom work particularly. I assure the minister it will cause many administrative headaches.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Two of the principles of taxation are ease of administration and equitable incidence, and I have pointed out how the proposed tax is both inequitable and difficult to administer. The minister is taking a regrettable step in extending this tax and I would urge him to withdraw it because it is going to cause a great deal of hardship across the country.
The minister may feel that he will collect more tax this way but I think he will collect less because a number of the tire retreaders who have spoken and written to me have indicated that since 1963 the sale of stock tires has decreased anywhere from 20 to 40 per cent. If that is the case, we are now going to reduce the sale of custom retread tires and encourage the purchase of new, cheap tires in the $9 to $12 range, on which the minister receives an 11 per cent tax on anywhere from 40 to 60 per cent of the value of those tires.
I think that the net revenue is going to decrease. Not only that, the minister will lose income tax revenue payable by these firms if employees are sacked or let go as a result of the step which he is taking. The whole thing is completely wrong and I urge the minister to withdraw this tax. I am sure the amount of revenue that will accrue to the crown from it will not be great. Yet its effect on a segment of industry will be especially harsh.

As I said earlier, the present law provides that stock retreads are taxed but custom retreads are not. This has produced a situation where as many tires as possible are brought in by motorists to be retreaded and are not subject to tax, to the detriment of

those companies which buy their own casings, retread them and sell them. That is the reason why we are proposing this amendment.
I admit the problem is a difficult one but I believe it should be possible through administrative means to deal fairly as between new tires and retread tires. I believe it should be possible through administrative practices to help in ensuring that these tires are taxed at approximately the same level of trade. I agree with the hon. member that it would not be equitable to have retread tires taxed at a level closer to the consumer than new tires would be taxed, and it may be possible through administrative means, as we do in many other industries, to maintain as much equity as possible.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a word or two on the bill to incorporate the Bank of British Columbia. A number of members from western Canada have expressed the opinion that we need more banking facilities in western Canada and banking executives who are more aware of the opportunities for investment in British Columbia and indeed in the other western provinces. I think that the Bank of British Columbia can help to perform this function. I think that the new Bank of British Columbia, like the Bank of Western Canada, will provide a more intimate knowledge of the resources of western Canada, of the market opportunities there as well as the export opportunities, as viewed from the vantage point of British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and, indeed, the Yukon and Northwest Territories.
There have been modifications over the last two years in the terms of the incorporation of the Bank of British Columbia which I think have been all to the good. The original plan was for the province of British Columbia to participate in the equity financing of the Bank of British Columbia. Initially, I believe the proposal was that the Crown, in right of the province of British Columbia, would put up 25 per cent of the equity capital and have voting privileges in porportion to that equity. This figure was later modified by the premier of British Columbia to 10 per cent.
Later the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) gave indications as to the nature of the amendments to the Bank Act as the act applies to the incorporation of chartered banks and their operations in this country, and one of the stipulations which the former minister of finance made over a year ago was that no government, be it foreign or provincial, should own equity shares in a chartered bank in Canada.
Private Bills
I understand that the amendments more recently made in the request for a charter for the Bank of British Columbia have taken this intention of the government of Canada, as expressed by the former minister of finance, into account and that the province of British Columbia does not now intend to own any equity shares in the Bank of British Columbia. In other words, there will be no ownership provisions and there will be no voting stock held by the province of British Columbia in the Bank of British Columbia.
I think this is all to the good. In this country we have a written constitution. We have powers reserved unto the provinces and the remaining powers, many of them very important and vital to the survival of this country as a nation, are reserved unto Canada as a whole.
One of the vital powers of this nation is control over money and banking, currency, the incorporation of banks and so on. I think it would be a pity if the parliament of Canada were ever in any way to delegate unto the provinces, and particularly unto one province, authority over banking or activities relating to banking in the sense of the activities of chartered banks. So that the retirement of the province of British Columbia from voting stock participation in this new chartered bank, the Bank of British Columbia, I think is a laudable move, one which all Canadians interested in the retaining of federal powers by the parliament of Canada and by Canada as a whole will appreciate.
There is another and important aspect to control of any corporation, of course, Mr. Speaker. One aspect is control over voting stock; another and equally important aspect, in the initial stages at least, is the appointment of directors. A list of directors appears in this bill to incorporate the Bank of British Columbia. Several of those directors are employees of the province of British Columbia. They are senior officers in Crown corporations established by the province of British Columbia.
In view of the expressed intention of the Minister of Finance of Canada that no other government, foreign or provincial, should have a substantial say in the policy-making of the chartered banks of this country, I personally wonder whether it is consistent with that intention to have paid officers of a provincial government on the board of directors of any chartered bank in Canada. I realize that this is an interim board, one which will be subject to the intentions of the

June 23, 1966
Private Bills
shareholders of the Bank of British Columbia. I presume that this particular subject will be thoroughly discussed when the Bank of British Columbia bill is referred to the committee of this house which deals with finance. Indeed, I am sure that the matter will be raised. It will be raised because one of the proposed directors is the chief fund raiser for the government party in the province of British Columbia.
To reiterate, Mr. Speaker, I welcome this incorporation. I believe we must incorporate this bank and more banks in western Canada. Certainly I welcome the incorporation of the Bank of British Columbia with headquarters in Vancouver, the directors of which are British Columbians, and with capital raised through private channels in the western part of the country. I am sure the bank will perform a vital function. Subject to the qualification which I raised in respect of the directors, I trust that this bill will pass first to the committee and then, when it comes back from committee, that the Bank of British Columbia bill will receive third reading so it can become one of the most prosperous and useful chartered banks in this country.

Mr. Speaker, before this bill is sent to the committee I should like to say a few words with regard to our banking system in relation to the bill.
Coming from a province in western Canada closely associated with British Columbia, I can say at the outset that I am in favour of a chartered bank with headquarters in British Columbia. However, like the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard I must speak about the directors of this bank. I would rather see the provincial government have a 10 per cent share in the bank, if this is necessary, than have it acquire control of the bank in a roundabout way. In other words, if the province is going to have an interest in the bank it should be so stated.
I spoke on a similar bill that came before the house in which it was provided that the province of British Columbia would have only a 10 per cent share interest in the proposed Bank of British Columbia.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
I said then that a bank charter is a very great privilege to be granted to any group of individuals and that a group granted such a charter should be prepared to work for the general advantage of Canada. A provincial premier certainly has responsibility for developing his province and providing for its people, and if he feels that an interest in a bank would help him to achieve those ends I cannot see why we should oppose an application along these lines.
However, as suggested by the previous speaker there is a close connection between the government and the directors set out in this bill. This makes one suspicious and I certainly hope that when the bill is sent to committee the members of that committee will carry out a thorough examination in this connection. Most hon. members do not like to see deals made under the table which might lead one to suspect there is or could be too close a connection. Before this parliament awards a charter to any group of individuals, careful consideration must be paid to their character, general worthiness and capacity to operate a bank.
It is interesting to note that last year there were three applications for charters on the order paper. One applicant is apparently

June 23, 1966
Private Bills
waiting until the revisions have been made to the Bank Act. This may be the proper attitude to take. Why apply for a charter before the act has been amended? Would it not be better to wait until we see the proposals for the revision of the Bank Act so that we will know exactly what we are granting?
A bank charter in this country is a privilege, and to appreciate this one must look at the banking situation over the years. Very few charters have been granted, none, in fact, since the thirties or a little earlier. But during the same period the house has dealt with many applications by finance companies, trust companies and people who in the minds of many might be classed as loan sharks. I do not think this is good for Canada. These loan companies do not need a charter from this house. Their accounts need not be subjected to federal scrutiny. Some hon. members might feel we should grant every application for a charter that is made. If we did we might find ourselves in the same position as many of the provinces with too many finance companies on shaky ground.
It is therefore our duty to give close scrutiny to every application for a charter. There should also be a careful examination of the worthiness and capacity of the directors, particularly as to their intent to work for the general advantage of Canada. A charter is a licence to operate in Canada as a private industry but with special privileges. We need only remember that banks today have a right to create money. That is what our banks do. For every dollar they have on deposit they can lend $20 or $30. This is a great privilege for a private business and we should make certain that the general intent is to work and serve for the advantage not necessarily of the board of directors or of the shareholders but of Canada as a whole. As it is, one does not know whether the province would have 50 per cent or 51 per cent of the influence, whether it would operate solely for the advantage of the

province, with its tremendous real and potential wealth in oil, timber and mineral resources, or whether it would work for the general good of the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to say that our group accepts this bill in principle; we are happy about its introduction and the fact that it is submitted by a province such as British Columbia.
Once this bill has been referred to the committee and passed by the house, it will be the first time in the history of parliament that a province has the right to operate a bank. That bank will belong to the province of British Columbia, if I understood the bill well.
Mr. Speaker, the provisions of the bill are not what we would like to see; we would like a much more flexible bill, granting much more common and stable rights, in short, rights which would give the province more powers than those which the bank exercises at the present time. But I know that British Columbia must comply with the government's requirements and accept the same conditions as the other banks.
The Bank Act will be the same for British Columbia as for any bank in Canada. But it is a step forward in the economy of the monetary and banking systems. If there is in that province capital to put at the disposal of the citizens, we must not be against the fact that such capital operates through a bank and that Canadians can benefit more therefrom.
The chartered banks are the creatures of the Canadian parliament. They literally owe their existence to it. They have to come to that same parliament every ten years to renew their charters without which they would stop existing. They get all their rights and privileges from parliament, even the exclusive right to create and issue money. That is so true that if the governmeht, as the sovereign body representing the whole nation, needs money in addition to what it gets from taxes or loans on the savings of the people, it must bow before those creatures.
June 23, 1966

Mr. Speaker, when that happens, it becomes obvious that the chartered banks are not constituted as they should be, because if the government is able to give them all that authority, it should at least hold the supreme authority and not be forced to go down on its knees before those institutions when it needs credit to finance the country. That is what we are against. We object to the fact that the government is forced to go down on its knees before the chartered banks and ask them to lend it money or credit to administer the business of the country when it has given them the exclusive right to create money and credit.
If the government can give these institutions exclusive rights, it can surely hold on to sovereign rights it has on institutions of its own creation and on the creation of money and credit in Canada. It is always a question of money, of shortage of money, when governments need credit. Not a single government in Canada, I would even say in the world, can create its own credit. Development of our various natural resources, construction of bridges, roads, institutions, universities, colleges, everything that is publicly-owned, should be financed and controlled by the sovereign government or a sovereign and independent commission of the government which would have control over money according to the ability of our citizens to develop our country.
There are many physical assets in this country which we could develop. The men are waiting; the institutions are waiting. Canada has a considerable number of engineers, qualified men capable of undertaking all those things Canadians absolutely need. We cannot do it because we operate within the money available, and we are too deep in debt. The federal and provincial governments are too deep in debt; the municipal governments and school boards are too deep in debt. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT TO PROVINCES OF CERTAIN CORPORATION INCOME TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution seeks the permission of this house for the introduction of a measure to provide for the payment to the provinces of 95 per cent of the income tax paid to the federal government by certain public utility corporations on that part of their income arising from their
June 23. 1966

public utility operations. An arrangement was made in 1947-and has been renewed periodically by succeeding governments-under which 50 per cent of this federal tax has been transferred to the provinces.
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)
In July last year the government undertook to increase the transfer from 50 per cent to 95 per cent and hon. members are being asked by this resolution to carry out this undertaking of the government of Canada.
The transfer to the provinces of a portion of the federal income tax paid by electrical, gas and steam utilities was instituted in 1947 as an integral part of the Dominion-Provincial Tax Rental Agreements Act of that year. Under that legislation Canada agreed to pay to the provinces for the five-year duration of the agreements one-half of the federal income tax paid by these utilities subject to certain minor adjustments. This sharing arrangement was continued for a further five years by the Tax Rental Agreements Act, 1952, and on the conclusion of that agreement Canada undertook at each subsequent quinquennial revision of the fiscal arrangements to continue the 50 per cent sharing by an item in the annual estimates.
In the estimates tabled in this house on February 14, 1966, there will be found under vote 5 of the Department of Finance a request for authority to share with the provinces the income tax paid by these utilities in 1964. It has, of course, been necessary over the years to adjust the regulations governing the 50 per cent sharing to take into account such changes in fiscal arrangements as the 1962 changeover from tax rental to tax collection agreements.
In addition to providing in 1947 for the payment to the provinces of one half of the income tax paid by certain privately owned public utilities, the government of Canada provided in the following year for a tax concession to these corporations. In 1948, at a time when the general tax rate was 50 per cent of taxable income, the rate on the taxable income of these public utilities was reduced to 43 per cent. While the 7 per cent rate advantage has been reduced, these corporations remain subject to a corporate income tax rate that remains 2 per cent less than the general 47 per cent corporate tax. This provision is contained in section 85 of the Income Tax Act. I draw this section to the attention of hon. members because many of the provisions of the bill which it is my intention to
Finance
introduce following the acceptance of this resolution are modelled on section 85 of the Income Tax Act.
The decision to increase this transfer to the provinces from 50 per cent to almost 100 per cent of the federal tax was in response to pressing representations from several provinces. Prior to and at the federal-provincial conference of prime ministers and premiers held in July last year many provinces argued that privately owned gas and electrical utilities were still at a competitive disadvantage vis-a-vis publicly owned utilities, and that this disadavantage inhibited the private companies from developing new power sites necessary for Canada's requirements. They also expressed concern that because of this differential treatment the customers of the privately owned utility companies were similarly placed at a disadvantage. Furthermore, it was argued that this disadvantage was felt most in those provinces which depended on private companies for the generation or distribution of electrical energy and gas and that the continuation of this disadvantage would oblige the provinces to consider the nationalization of these utilities. The government of Canada was obliged to acknowledge, after careful consideration, the force of the provincial argument as to the effect upon the consumers of electrical energy and gas of the differential treatment of utilities.
In announcing the policy decision to increase the tax transfer to the provinces my predecessor, the hon. member for Davenport, indicated that while the federal transfers to the provinces would continue to be unconditional he expected that the provinces would ensure that the benefit of the increased transfer would be passed on to consumers in the form of reduced rates.
Before speaking further to the intent of this resolution I should like to explain the 95 per cent figure. Hon. members may wonder why the government did not undertake to transfer 100 per cent of the federal tax to the provinces. The reason is that the federal government needs to retain some 5 per cent of the federal tax revenue to compensate it for the dividend tax credit it continues to give to shareholders of these Canadian corporations.
The public utility corporations to which this resolution applies are those whose main business is the distribution and sale to the public of electrical energy, gas and steam or the generation and sale for distribution to the public of electrical energy and steam. It is

June 23. 1966
Finance
the federal income tax paid by these corporations that this resolution proposes to transfer to the provinces. Hon. members may find it helpful if I were to refer to the relevant provisions of the Income Tax Act.
Part I, section 85, of the Income Tax Act, to ensure that the 45 per cent rate applies only to corporations that are genuinely in the public utility field and does not extend to corporations that may, incidental to their main activity, generate or sell electrical energy, gas or steam, requires that a corporation to be eligible for the lower rate must receive more than one half of its total gross revenue from such distribution and sale or generation and sale. Similarly, part I of the Income Tax Act, to ensure that the lower rate of taxation does not apply to corporations that are merely providing electrical energy, gas or steam mainly for subsidiaries or parent companies, and are not serving the public, requires that a corporation to be eligible for the preferred tax rate must receive more than one half of its gross revenues from sales to persons with whom it deals at arm's length.
The resolution now before this house seeks to secure the consent of hon. members to the introduction of a bill which will incorporate conditions analogous to the above provisions in part I of the Income Tax Act. I should further explain that where a corporation qualifies under the Income Tax Act for the preferred rate, that rate applies only to that portion of the corporation's income that arises from its distribution and sale or generation and sale to the public. It is 95 per cent of this portion of the qualifying corporation's federal tax that this resolution seeks the permission of the committee to pay to the provinces. When the 95 per cent share of the federal tax is determined, that amount will be paid to the province or provinces in which the distribution and sale or generation and sale to the public is made.
The resolution also proposes that the 95 per cent sharing arrangements shall apply to the income tax paid by the eligible corporations on income earned after December 31, 1965. It is the government's intention to continue to apply the present 50 per cent sharing arrangements to the tax paid on income earned up to and including December 31, 1965. As I previously stated, the estimates for 1966-67 tabled in this house on February 14 contain a provision to cover taxation years ending in the 1964 calendar year, and authority will be requested in the 1967-68 estimates to continue the existing arrangements in respect of the

1965 calendar year. Hon. members will note that there is a delay of approximately two years between the taxation year in which the profits are earned and the year in which the 50 per cent share is paid to the provinces. Aside from the time lag allowed all corporations in the filing of their tax returns, further delay is occasioned by the need to identify those corporations in respect of which the 50 per cent sharing arrangement applies and then to re-process their tax returns to determine the amount of tax revenues to be shared and the province or provinces to whom payment is to be made.
Mr. Chairman, in concluding my remarks, I should point out that when the government of Canada undertook to pay to the provinces 95 per cent of the federal income tax paid by these public utilities, it attached no conditions to the payments. My predecessor, the hon. member for Davenport, did express the expectation, as did Hon. Donald Fleming when in his 1961 budget speech he announced the continuation of the half-sharing arrangements, that the provinces might wish to use the additional revenue for the benefit of the industry and its customers. I also hope that the provinces will use the federal tax transfer for the benefit of the industry and its customers.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am very
pleased to see this resolution on the order paper. I can say that I thoroughly approve of it. I recall that in 1963, 1964, and I believe in 1965 I and other Alberta members in particular made representations in this regard, because of all provinces in Canada the province of Alberta will be affected, generally, more than any other. This is particularly the case with regard to electric power because apart from the municipal generation plant in the city of Edmonton, most of the electric power produced and consumed in the province of Alberta is by private companies.
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)
We also have the distribution of natural gas in Alberta, so that province is very conscious of the sources of its power, just as any other province would be. It has always
June 23. 1966

been felt that the incidence of this income tax on Alberta Power Corporation placed the province at some disadvantage in competition with other provinces for the location of industry based on favourable power rates, because these other provinces had nationalized their hydro, in particular. As a matter of fact, I think it is common knowledge that Premier Bennett in 1961 nationalized B.C. Electric because he had not been able to get this particular increment from 50 per cent to either 95 per cent or 100 per cent, which he felt was his due. Well, the people of British Columbia now have a nationalized hydro system whether they like it or not, and they can thank Premier Bennett for that. This was one of those great whirlabouts. He was for free enterprise and private ownership, except where it suited his particular purpose.
I am glad to say that in so far as the province of Alberta is concerned, the wishes of the Minister of Finance and his predecessor in regard to this have been passed on by the provincial government. After all, the province need pass on these benefits to no particular company, and any particular company need not pass them on to its customers. The end result, however, so far as Alberta is concerned, has been that the province, after some hesitation but not long, did agree that all benefits derived by the province as a result of this agreement with the federal government, and which we are now asked to approve, would be passed on to the power companies concerned. This same, shall we say, message has been passed on to the companies. I am sure that this will result in either an actual reduction of rates or will prevent-and this is what is vitally important as well-predictable applications to the various utility commissions for increases in rates. I know one private company is on its third wage increase this year as a result of the incidence of the Canada Pension Plan and a number of other things. These costs cannot be paid out of thin air. They have to be paid ultimately out of earnings based on their utility rates, and in order to get an increase in those rates these companies have to go before their respective utility commissions. This provision will help defer some of the increasing expenses of power corporations.
We will be interested in seeing just what the provisions will be in the bill. I know that there are a number of provinces, particularly those which do have natural gas distribution companies, which will be affected by this provision. Others, I believe Nova Scotia is
Finance
likely the only other one, will have privately owned power systems and they, too, should benefit. I agree with the minister that the house should accept this resolution and that we should see the bill as soon as possible.

speechtext:
I rise, Mr. Chairman, to oppose this resolution and its principle as being, in my opinion, contrary to the best interests of the people of Canada in all parts of this country. I think it is a wrong principle, although it is already on the statute books, because constantly, in my experience, private corporations that function in the same field as public enterprise are always complaining about the fact that they have to pay taxes and public corporations do not. I have heard that complaint by private corporations in the field of transportation and in the field of communications where there are publicly owned enterprises.
Furthermore, Mr. Chairman, I think the
time has come for us to recognize that even though it is up to the people in each province to do as they pleased, all public utilities ought to be publicly owned. Whatever the reason may have been for Premier Bennett of British Columbia to bring the corporation there under public ownership, he did a service to the people of his province, just as the Lesage government did for the people of Quebec by bringing Hydro Quebec under public control. I do not believe this parliament ought to do anything to encourage a continuation of the private exploitation of basic public utilities that are the foundation of all economic and industrial activity in every part of the country.
My third point-I am putting them briefly because I do not want to make a long speech-is that I do not accept that the hope the minister expressed will be realized. In fact, if I understood his explanation correctly, he will make these rebates to the provinces concerned unconditionally. The provinces concerned may or may not hand them on to private corporations. I have no doubt that they will, but of course they are not obliged to do so. If he makes these rebates on the basis of tax arrangements with the provinces, I am sure he will agree with me that is the worst possible way in which to deal with so important a matter as the division of tax revenues. If he is making this rebate to the provinces to help the people concerned obtain cheaper electricity or cheaper gas, there is simply no guarantee whatever that will occur. The province may hand that money over

June 23. 1966
Finance
to the corporation but there is no guarantee that the corporation will in turn hand the benefit over to the consumers of the utility. If they don't, Mr. Chairman, parliament will have been responsible for adding to the very large profits now made by corporations who are crying tears about the extra federal income taxes they have to pay.
I see no reason why this parliament and the people of Canada as a whole should give up some of the revenue collected from corporation income tax in order to favour the private corporations' profit margin. There might be some sense to it if there were some way of guaranteeing that these benefits would be handed over to the consumers by the private utility corporations. I have no guarantee whatever that that will be done, nor has the minister. He expresses the hope that will happen. He expresses the hope that provincial authorities concerned will express the hope that will happen. This is about where he is and about where hon. members of this house are with regard to the likelihood of these benefits being handed on to the consumers.
As I suggested, Mr. Chairman, over most of the world and over most of Canada, the overwhelming majority of the units concerned with the manufacture and distribution of electricity and gas are now under public ownership. I know gas is not to the same extent, but it will be in the not too distant future, and that is where it ought to be. Public utilities ought to be under the control of the people, through their legislatures and parliament.
[DOT] (7:30 p.m.)
I oppose with all the vigour I can this added piece of pie to corporations which are already exploiting the natural resources of this country to their benefit, and who can afford to reduce their rates to compete with public corporations simply by reducing the cut of profit which they now get. My memory from looking at the figures is that private utility corporations are doing very well after taxes despite the fact that they pay this income tax. I see no reason why this parliament and the people of Canada should give them an additional handout.

I may say, again in the same vein as I spoke on the resolution stage, that this is but part of the broader prospect of farm legislation which we hope and believe will bring the farmer into a more equitable position in the economy respective to his counterpart in industry who, during the past few years, with the industrial progress which has been made in this country, has moved ahead economically at a very rapid pace. On the other hand, I think the farmer has been equally productive. Statistics indicate that farm production has increased on a per capita basis at an even more rapid rate than industrial production in this age of automation. Despite that fact, I do not think that the farmer's economic position has kept pace with his productivity as a producer under our economic system. We have all heard many times in the past few months that the farmer finds himself caught in this price-cost squeeze where, even though he has become much more productive, the costs of the things he must buy have gone ahead far more rapidly than the price he can receive for his produce. This may be inevitable in a society that is progressing rapidly industrially. We have come up very rapidly industrially. Costs of industrial production go up. It is all to the good that there be higher wages in industry and higher returns for industry. However, on the one hand the farmer is caught by the fact that he must pay the prices that are concomitant with this fast development in the industrial world, while at the same time the price of the food he produces-some of which is sold domestically, and other of which, particularly in respect of that from western Canada which finds its way to world markets-has not kept up with the costs of the things that he must buy.
I think we would all agree that the farmer's income has not kept pace with that of his industrial counterpart. At the same time, two or three decades ago Canadians generally had not achieved the standard of living that they have today. Today we accept as necessities things that 30 or 40 years ago might have been looked upon as luxuries.
But the farmer, caught in this cost-price squeeze also, as are other citizens, expects greater social and economic returns from the fruits of his endeavour. He wants to have the things that his city counterpart has, and there is no reason why he should not have those things that are looked upon as the just rights and deserts of citizens today. I think the
Stabilization of Milk and Cream Prices farmer, caught in the cost-price squeeze, is not enabled to have the income which is comparable to his city counterpart's, as was the case pre-war. On the other hand the farmer is expected to be able to provide for his family in just as satisfactory a fashion, just as adequately, as his city counterpart. Therefore he finds himself caught on both sides of the horn of this dilemma.
Accordingly, I think that all agricultural legislation must be aimed to the end of enabling the producer to have a more adequate, more suitable and more reliable income. We are all concerned that in certain segments of the agricultural community there is a diminishing number of producers, and that not as many young people are going into farming as we should like to see. It is therefore the function of government to see to it that we have policies that will give adequate and suitable returns to the farmer, and that the profession of agriculture, and the family farm as we know it, or as it will develop in future, will provide an adequate return and an enticing way of life to our young people in the future.
I stated earlier, at the resolution stage, that in this regard I think it is necessary for us to go ahead on a threefold front. First, I think it is inevitable that if the family farm is to be maintained, to provide the kind of income of which I spoke earlier, that it must be a viable economic entity. It must be more a business than merely a social way of life, which was the way of the past. This requires larger capitalization for land, machinery, chemicals, fertilizer, etc. The family farm unit must be more heavily capitalized than was the case in the past.
Inasmuch as the private sector of the economy has not seen fit or been able to provide the capital for the farmer to expand as he needs to, then surely it is the function of government to provide this capital. We have tried to do something along these lines m an earlier measure. I am speaking of the farm credit corporation.
Second, it is of no value to have a viable economic unit if you do not have adequate and suitable markets. This piece of legislation is geared to this marketing aspect, which has always been such a bugbear in Canada by virtue of the complexities of our constitution, and which has resulted in marketing being a field requiring co-operative action with respect to legislation. Intraprovincial marketing is, of course, by virtue of judicial decisions

June 23, 1966
respecting our constitution, a provincial matter.
On the other hand, many facets of marketing have an extraprovincial or extraterritorial effect. Therefore the federal government must play its proper and adequate part. In the area of marketing, to provide suitable markets and reasonable and adequate returns to the farmer we are proposing the bill that is before the house at this time, in the interests of the dairy industry. In particular it is important to point out that the stability of income that we desire for dairy farmers is not only to redound to the benefit of producers. There has been too great a tendency, because of our becoming a more urban country, with a larger percentage of our population every day, every week, every month moving into the cities, for us not to appreciate the farmer's viewpoint. His viewpoint has not been sufficiently understood or appreciated by much of our urban population.
I point out that a measure such as this, which is a step toward responsible marketing legislation with respect to a particular segment of the agricultural community, also does a very considerable service to the consumers in the urban centres, because it is intended to bring closer the day when there will not be these inevitable rises and falls in production and in price which, when they reach one end of the scale, swing around, inevitably to the detriment of the consumer. At the end of the swing, when production becomes reduced and prices go up, because there is no control over production, by reason of the lack of adequate marketing legislation, it is the consumer who pays. When prices go up, that certainly is not in the interests of the consumer. When that happens we get into the old cycle, and up goes production with higher prices. This sort of thing has been the bane of the agricultural community in the past.
The marketing aspect of the measure is meant to encourage stability, and a reasonable return for the farmer. This is an extremely important measure. I believe this is the first measure, should it be passed by parliament, enabling the national marketing of a commodity such as dairy products. I think we will all watch with interest, if this house sees fit to pass the measure, to see how it works out, and to see whether it does the job required with respect both to the consumer's needs and the producer's income. Because if this measure does what we believe it will do, it may be that the house will see fit in the years to come to bring other agricultural

June 23, 1966

products within legislation of this type, which will enable national marketing of other agricultural products on an adequate scale, in co-operation with the provinces.
[DOT] (7:50 p.m.)
I suggest that the way toward a more stable farm income and a better development of our agricultural community might well be through this type of national marketing legislation. I would say a word, also, with respect to the third aspect of sound agricultural legislation, that is, legislation to protect the farmer against drought or other calamity. In this connection we are, of course, presenting a crop insurance amendment so that the three aspects of fundamental agricultural need might be covered.
I do not wish in any way to belittle these measures to aid the problems which affect the agricultural community in our country. I do not say these measures are all that are needed-not by a long shot. I had the honour of attending as a witness before the agricultural committee of this house. This is an exercise which would be difficult for one much more expert than I am in agricultural matters. But my attendance did impress upon me very strongly a feeling I had held previously: the knowledgeable and experienced members of that committee all seemed concerned about the need for over-all direction in Canadian agricultural policy.
Measures that provide for crop insurance, orderly marketing and so on are important moves in the right direction. But I do not wish to leave the thought that this is all that is required by the agricultural community. Agricultural development in this country has been one of evolution. It has come about largely as a result of the individual initiative and individual requirements of farmers across the land with respect to their profit motivation. I do not believe there has been any comprehensive over-all planning of our agricultural growth during the years of our history. We have moved as the times seemed to require and as individuals saw best with respect to the profitable operation of their own entities. In these dynamic times in which we are living today, all of us, certainly those of us who are on this side of the house, are convinced that a great degree of planning and direction is needed if we are to achieve the most productive and profitable results from the various segments of our economic endeavour, including agriculture.
It is not easy to get at the fundamentals of agricultural need. We are all aware that the
23033-433i
Stabilization of Milk and Cream Prices sphere of agriculture is vested in both provincial and federal governments and legislatures, and apart from measures such as this, which are patently in the right direction, I am very much of a mind that in the not-too-distant future the provinces, the federal government, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the farm unions and all the bodies which represent agriculture across the country will find it necessary to get together to work out a broad, new, long-term prospect for Canadian agriculture. I believe this is badly needed.
In the short period during which I have had the honour to hold this portfolio I have not yet reached conclusions as to whether we are doing the right things in the right places -whether we are growing the right crops in the right quantities. I think a broad inquiry of this kind is needed. We need to protect the domestic requirements of our agricultural community in the future, bearing in mind the growth of the domestic population, bearing in mind the new affluence of our society, and the necessity for our agricultural products being acceptable to the changing tastes of the community.
All these things must be considered to determine, in the domestic interest, what would be best for Canadian agriculture in the next two or three decades. We need long-range planning in this direction. There is an equally important requirement with respect to our national responsibilities-the part we should play in the next decade or so and the responsibilities we should assume with respect to the world food supply and our share of the commitment to world production. Statistics indicate that if we are to hold our own in our ability to supply the world with cereals we shall have to double cereal production by 1980. When we consider that the world population will double by the end of this century, and since we all believe that society as a whole must do a much better job of feeding the world than it has in the past, surely Canada, which has such abilities and resources in this sphere, will have to play a bigger part and make a larger commitment to the world community generally.
Here again, I believe there must be a pervasive national planning to determine how in the coming decades we shall be able to play our full and just part in this area as well as with respect to our domestic responsibilities.
I hope hon. gentlemen opposite will support this measure which, as I say, I believe to be a

There are, however, one or two clauses to which I intend to make reference. Over the years I have heard from those sitting opposite about the dangers of protection. When in opposition the Liberal party always stood against protection, and when in office it carried out the policies it had condemned. Here is a very interesting portion of this particular bill:
The governor in council may include on the import control list . . . any dairy product the import of which he deems it necessary to control for the purpose of implementing any action taken under this act to support the price of that dairy product or that has the effect of supporting the price of that dairy product.
That is a tremendous power for the governor in council to exercise-the power to assure that by order in council the government may at any time prevent the importation of any dairy product into Canada. Certainly powers like this will have to be exercised with discretion and care. These powers should not be exercised except when our neighbour to the south endeavours to dispose of any surplus in Canada to the detriment of our price level within this country. In other words, while that clause has in it the essence of protection, it can be used effectively only if in its use there is a realization of the fact that that use should be sparingly utilized, and only for the purpose of protecting and preserving the prices in Canada against the invasion of surpluses form other countries.

Here is another power. The purposes and objects of the legislation in the setting up of the commission are to provide efficient producers of milk and cream with the opportunity of obtaining a fair return for their labour and investment, and to provide consumers of dairy products with a continuous and adequate supply of dairy products of high quality. If my information is correct, our dairy production will not meet the needs of Canadians within the next couple of years. Farmers in the dairy business no longer see any purpose in remaining in an agricultural production which denies them a fair and proper return.
That brings me to a matter with which the minister dealt, namely the squeeze in which the farmer finds himself. There is the rising cost of production; labour costs are very high and there is the difficulty in obtaining the necessary labour on the farm; and the price of machinery has gone up to an extent which cannot be justified. The only action taken by the government to date is the setting up of a commission of one man to look into this matter. After two and a half [Mr. Dielenbaker.l

I say to the minister that all the legislation which has been placed on the statute books will be a nullity unless there is effective action taken to meet the tremendous increase in the cost of machinery. This is where the farmer is in a dilemma today. He has no protection; he sells on the open market and he buys on a market that denies to him reasonable and fair prices. Finally who suffers? It is the consumer.
If action is taken which raises the prices of farm products to a height that would be unjust, those who suffer are the consumers of this nation. Today they are paying through the nose. I am one of those who believe that the family farm can be preserved in Canada and that we can have a certain kind of efficiency along with that policy. So I go right back, as I always have, to saying that the underlying principle that we should keep in mind is the preservation of the family farm, the small farm. Whenever you pick up an article on agriculture in Canada today you are inclined to read how well off a certain segment of the agricultural industry happens to be. We have thousands and thousands of marginal farms, and when I say marginal farms I do not mean necessarily that the land is not productive but that the size and location of the farm, its credit rating and the labour situation on it puts it into the category of being an uneconomic unit.
I do not go along with ministers of agriculture or experts in the Department of Agriculture who say that larger and more efficient farm units is the only answer for Canadian agriculture. I say quite the reverse, that the only answer for Canadian agriculture is a very, very widely spread agricultural industry on as many small, family farm units as this country can possibly support. Therefore I agree that there must be a certain amount of planning, but any planning in Canada which tends to reduce the number of farmers on the land and concentrates only on the so-called cost per cent per unit, to the farmer's detriment and the detriment of the welfare of Canada, is in my opinion the wrong type of planning.

The need for such an authority, or "commission" as the government prefers to call it, arises out of technological advances.
