Price and marketing policy, including price support; the policy problems created by new products: changing structures in both the farming and processing sectors of the industry; planning of dairy export policy-all of these matters have led to the urgent need for the development of new, coordinated dairy policy through the establishment of appropriate boards or commissions.
The co-ordination must not only be between policies at provincial level, but between provincial and federal policies.
So, Mr. Speaker, I believe it is evident that

The present system has led them to bankruptcy because you favoured farm loans and all the farms are mortgaged. Is that commission going to pull them out of the clutches of financiers? Never. The farmers know their own needs; just read their brief. The Department of Agriculture and all its agronomists must know what to do. You must know the needs of the farmers; there is no need to create a new commission.

It has long been considered to establish commissions in order to settle the problem, to spend the taxpayers' money, to tax the people even more, the workers, the builders of the country, so as to pay some gentlemen $25,000 a year. speechtext:
I rise, Mr. Speaker, to put a question again which I put
June 23, 1966
in the house on June 13-perhaps that is the reason no answer was given. The question had to do with a very important speech delivered by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) on the previous Saturday, I believe, when he received the Pioneer Award at Springfield, in the United States. The substance of the question was whether, in the light of the Prime Minister's remarks on that Saturday afternoon he was recommending, or his government was going to recommend at some future date, a federal union of north Atlantic countries which would provide for some kind of collective political and economic policies.
Now, on rereading the speech I discovered that it had a great deal to say not only about some far reaching plans with regard to the economic union of the north Atlantic countries, but there was a strong suggestion made of the possibility of an even wider union including, at some far distant point in time, the union of all countries. Whether or not the Prime Minister was suggesting here some kind of world union or federation, he did not make it abundantly clear. He did say a number of other things, however, that seem to be relevant to our situation vis-a-vis NATO. One of the things he said which has not been reacted to very much in our country to date was that perhaps of all countries presently faced with the problem of NATO, France is most realistic in accepting the fact that the kind of agreements that were made in the late forties with regard to north Atlantic defence may not have the same viability and reality today that they had at that time.
By contrast, he also indicated that some of the more powerful nations making up NATO, I think by inference indicating our neighbour to the south, were not being altogether too realistic in their own reactions to the new position of France with regard to the NATO alliance. Indeed the Prime Minister went so far as to say that NATO itself is certainly not sacrosanct, and we must think of NATO in new terms and new leadership and in the sense of a greater amount of autonomy amongst the European nations. Perhaps we may even have to have a period of suspended animation, so to speak, when the European nations can consolidate their own strength, and then we can enter into some kind of far-reaching union. When we talk about the ways in which technology and the mass media draw closer together, it is interesting to think that perhaps there are new and
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion different alternatives to the inward looking nationalism that has been part and parcel of the western world, particularly at certain difficult times in the last 50 years.
I, myself, am most anxious to see a wider public debate take place, not only in this house but in the nation, as to the possibility of new kinds of relationships, economically and politically, with nations on both sides of the Atlantic. I quote from the Prime Minister's speech:
It is essential that we move ahead in the field of political and social organization in a way which is at least remotely comparable to our technological and scientific progress ...
I repeat, we must develop common, unifying political institutions which would provide for collective foreign and economic policies, as well as genuinely collective defence.
I am more than anxious to hear the response of either the Prime Minister or his representative here this evening.

Mr. Speaker, on June 14 I directed a question to the President of the Privy Council regarding

June 23, 1966

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion the pricing and sales policies of gasoline companies in many parts of the country. The question was prompted in view of the recent report of the royal commission on the gasoline price structure in the province of British Columbia, which indicated the existence of unfair trade practices.
I asked the minister whether he would give serious consideration to conducting an immediate investigation under the Combines Investigation Act into the pricing, marketing and production practices of the oil, gasoline and products industry. I based the urgency of the question on the situation which prevailed in my riding at the time, where the gasoline dealers, in despair and anger at the situation current in the industry, had decided to close down their pumps for one day in protest. This was a mood that was sweeping many parts of Ontario. Other gasoline dealers had closed down the day before and there was an indication that others were prepared to continue this kind of shut-down to register their protest at the pricing practices of the oil companies in Canada.
I am pleased to see the President of the Privy Council here tonight to reply to my question. With all due consideration for him I might say that the answer he gave in reply to my question did not give me encouragement in regard to his willingness to accept the urgency of an investigation into this situation. I am, of course, looking forward to hearing a further statement from him tonight.
In this particular case the gasoline dealers in the riding of Waterloo South have, I feel, performed a signal public service in bringing this matter to attention. I should like to quote a statement made by the president of the Association of Gasoline Dealers in Waterloo South which appeared in the Evening Reporter of Saturday, June 11. The president, Mr. Lester, said:
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
The majority of the driving public is taking a terrible beating from the companies on the price of gas-"We hate to sell it at 44-45 cents a gallon. There is no need for that price. They are becoming too greedy . . . and are fleecing the public."
At present, he said, the companies are charging Galt area dealers 38 cents a gallon for retail gas. "To get our 7.9 cents a gallon profit, which is not that large, we have to sell at 44.45 cents," he said. "At the same time, they sell it to unbranded dealers at 30-31 cents-who can re-sell it at about what we are paying."
He went on to say:
"'If it is being sold at 31 cents to unbranded dealers, we intend to apply pressure to get the

same price," said Mr. Lester, "At present, the situation is completely unfair." Even at that price, 31 cents, he stated, the companies are making a solid profit on auto gasoline, which is a comparatively cheap product to manufacture.
He claimed about 90 per cent of the retail station gas outlets were owned and operated by the companies, "who believe they can charge them any price they like."
"Their attitude is that, if we don't like it, we can get out of the business," he protested. This was a bad situation when many dealers had invested money and their livelihood in equipment and facilities.
The problem of gasoline prices in Canada is serious not only for the dealers involved, who I genuinely believe are working very hard for small remuneration, and who are frequently little more than serfs of the oil companies, but also for the public. There are indications that the price of gasoline in Canada is far higher than it should be. There are indications that our national oil policy, apart from its effects on the consumer, is working to the detriment of Canada; that it is not helping to reduce our balance of payments problem; and that because the oil companies in Canada are completely protected from foreign competition, the prices they charge are what the traffic will carry.
One needs only look at what has been going on in Canada to see how inefficient this industry is in looking after the public welfare. We must ask, do we need gasoline stations on nearly every corner of a metropolitan area? Also, who pays for these gasoline stations? In answering, I suggest that the public is paying for them, and that the station operators at the same time are being put into a most difficult situation in terms of earning their own living. The implications from the overbuilding that has been going on are that the cost of stations is being passed on to the public, which must pay for the high overheads in the industry.
Many other aspects of the problem could be raised, but time does not permit me to do so. I raise this question because I think it is incumbent upon the President of the Privy Council, who is head of the new department that is supposed to assume responsibility for consumer affairs, to institute a complete and wide ranging investigation in this whole problem.
One province in particular has already done this, and has come up with interesting findings. That province has made certain charges that I think the new department should investigate. But any province is restricted in the investigation it can conduct.

The hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Saltsman) has, in fact, urged me to cause an inquiry to be undertaken by the combines branch into the oil industry with respect to pricing, marketing and production of oil and gasoline products.
It is, of course, apparent that this is a matter of some public concern, as witness an inquiry by a royal commission in the province of British Columbia and the pressure for other inquiries at the provincial level which are in progress or are forecast.
The undertaking of such an industry-wide study is a large-scale project. Hon. members will be aware that within the past few years the Director of Investigation and Research has undertaken an inquiry into certain aspects of this industry which resulted in the publication, in 1962 of the T.B.A. report by the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission.
Clearly there are a number of important industries in Canada concerning which research studies might well be undertaken, and different views are no doubt held as to which sectors of the economy ought to be examined by way of research, and the priority to be assigned to various studies. Unfortunately, the research section of the combines branch cannot physically undertake all the projects that hon. members would suggest and, indeed, it must develop its program in an orderly manner and in accordance with the best judgment of the officials concerned in the light of the staff available.
I have already drawn to the attention of the director the suggestion of the hon. member for Waterloo South. The director has

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion came from this side or from dissident Liberals, by saying, "Wait for the Canada Assistance Plan. It is going to have something in it for old age pensioners, perhaps even more than the opposition is asking for."
I hope the parliamentary secretary is not going to give that answer tonight because we have now got the bill that sets out the Canada Assistance Plan and we know there is not in it any direct benefit to any old age security recipient. It provides for payments to the provinces on a certain basis, and if the provinces decide to supplement pensioners' income on a needs test basis, the federal government will share in the cost. But there is no increase in the pension itself.
This is a retrograde step about which we will have something to say on Monday when the Canada Assistance Plan is before us, but I say to the parliamentary secretary and the government, do not give us that line any longer. What both she and other Liberals on that side know is that there needs to be in this session an increase in the old age security pension at least to $100 a month across the board. Prices are going up. People are facing real problems in this area, and this parliament stands on trial on the question of whether or not it is going to meet the needs of our older people.
I make just one more comment. I suppose I should be chivalrous and say the parliamentary secretary is not old enough to remember what I am going to refer to, but I would like to remind Liberal members that the last time a Liberal government was defeated at the polls, which was in 1958, it was defeated largely because of its callous attitude to the old age pensioners. I am beginning to wonder whether the same Liberal party is not trying to court another defeat on the same issue. Despite all its talk nothing is being done to meet the needs of our older people. This is a crying shame.

I hope we are going to get legislation in this field. I hope the rumours that there are ructions in the Liberal party are true. I hope we are going to get legislation at this session. If the parliamentary secretary cannot tell us that this is the case, then I warn her that the party she supports has a very rough road ahead, and so it should, if it does not do better for the old age pensioners of this country.
